name: Enhancing access to continued learning in a pandemic

content.title: Enhancing access to continued learning in a pandemic
content.summary: IED, EA conducts a study that aims to help children catch up on lost time during closure of schools

media.caption: Teacher creating learning materials during the teacher training workshop at Nachingwea Teachers Training College in Tanzania
media.alt: Enhancing access to continued learning in a pandemic

content.text: Following closure of schools due to the COVID-19 pandemic, AKU's Institute for Educational Development East Africa (IED, EA) conducted a research intervention in Lindi region, Tanzania. The project knows as 'COVID-19 Emergence Rapid Response Intervention' was aimed at empowering headteachers, teachers and parents to help children catch up with lost time and continue learning.

The six-month project which closed in December 2020, worked with 50 primary public schools in five districts in the Lindi region: Lindi MC, Nachingwea, Liwale, Ruangwa and Kilwa. Various strategic initiatives were employed at this time.

"We designed, printed and distributed curriculum materials to guide lower primary school teachers through accelerated learning pedagogies. We also designed, developed and distributed head teachers' toolkits intended to help them with leadership skills during emergency situations, and in addition, conducted intensive training to both teachers and head teachers on how to use the toolkit to support accelerated learning in their institutions," said DrAbdallah Mohamed, lead investigator and faculty member at IED EA.

More than 70 head teachers, 200 primary school teachers and 11,500 students benefited from the project.In addition to dissemination of the learning materials and training of teachers, the intervention also involved empowering parents with skills to support their children's learning at home after reopening of schools, engaging social workers in supporting students with mental health after reopening of schools, and also sensitize communities about issues related to children protection and gender responsive care during and after pandemic.

"Preliminary findings show a positive impact on children learning due to improved learning environment. This is attributed to increased teacher competency and confidence in using accelerated learning approach, improved teacher competency in designing, developing and using suitable resources and using appropriate assessment practices," said Dr Winston Massam course facilitator and faculty member at IED, EA.

The findings also showed improved capacity and practice by the head teachers to monitor the teaching and learning process; fostering collaboration with other stakeholders, such as parents, community development officers and community welfare officers; and an improved school physical environment that supported children's quality learning.

There was also improvement in parents' competencies and practice in supporting children's learning at home where quite a number of parents gave evidence of providing their children with time to attend to assignments and helping them with their studies.Psychosocial support for children and parents affected by COVID -19 pandemic increased, as parents got connected with social welfare personnel who would attend to their issues.

This project intervention, carried out in June 2020, enabled the teachers in southern Tanzania to continue offering quality primary education despite the pandemic. It allowed them to complete their academic syllabuses and thus providing a conducive learning environment for students. IED, EA as a key stakeholder in education continues to offer support to schools through education systems strengthening in Tanzania.
